title: Big questions
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Me alegro de que + haya + V-participle

rules.text: A trigger of EMOTION or VALUE with a person inside it takes the subjunctive in the clause after it: me alegro de que vengas, me molesta que la gente no escuche, es una pena que no vinieran. L4-M4 bought the impersonal judgement (es importante que); what is new is that somebody is now doing the feeling.

The subjunctive only appears when the two halves have DIFFERENT subjects. When the person feeling and the person doing are the same, Spanish drops the que and takes the infinitive: me alegro de venir, not me alegro de que vengo. That is the minimal pair of this module and it never bends.

The TENSE of the subjunctive is chosen by the trigger, not by you. Present trigger, present subjunctive: me molesta que digan. Present trigger about something already done, perfect subjunctive: me alegro de que hayas venido. Past trigger, imperfect subjunctive: me molesto que dijeran.

Lo plus an adjective makes an abstract noun out of nothing: lo importante, lo bueno, lo dificil, lo malo. It is how Spanish names a quality it has no noun for, and it is the opener that abstract talk runs on: lo importante es que, and then the claim.

English uses the indicative under every single one of these triggers — I am glad you are coming — so nothing at all warns you that a choice is due. Me alegro de que vienes is the commonest error of this level, and it is invisible to the ear that made it.

English has no lo. The important thing is a noun phrase with a dummy noun inside it, so a learner builds la cosa importante and is understood, and permanently marked. There is no noun in the Spanish at all: lo does the work a noun would do.

Register: an English speaker hedges an abstract claim to be polite — I suppose one might say. Spanish states the claim flat and hedges the FRAME instead: en el fondo, la verdad es que. L3-M3 and L4-M4 each said this; this is the third and last time, and it is the same law.

The machinery is here and the belief is yours. Nothing in this module argues for a position, and none of these topics is small talk with somebody you have just met: they are the two-in-the-morning conversation and the panel, and the address follows the scene.

sentences.display: Lo importante es que la gente escuche, no que tenga razón.
sentences.cue: The important thing is that people listen, not that they are right.
sentences.literal: The important it-is that the people they-may-listen, not that they-may-have reason.

words.note: L4-M5 taught importante. Lo turns the bare adjective into a noun with no noun in it: the important thing, said in two words.
L3-M10 taught gente. It is singular in Spanish however many people it means, so the verb after it is singular: la gente escuche, not escuchen.
Present subjunctive of escuchar, sitting under lo importante es que. The -ar verb takes an -e ending here, the mirror of its indicative -a.

sentences.trap: La gente is singular. Every verb hanging off it is singular too, and this is the agreement an English speaker gets wrong first and longest.
sentences.sound: Escuche is es-CU-che; the initial e is fully pronounced, so it is not skoo-che.

variations.display: Lo importante es que la gente escuche.
variations.cue: What matters is that people listen.
variations.changed: The claim without its contrast, which is the shape the pattern actually has: lo plus adjective, es que, then the claim.

mistake.display: La cosa importante es que la gente escucha.
mistake.why: Two errors, and both are English showing through. There is no noun in the Spanish — lo importante, never la cosa importante — and es que here takes the subjunctive, escuche.

sentences.usage: Neutral. This is the opener of nearly every abstract claim in Spanish, and it works in a seminar and at a kitchen table without changing a word.
sentences.mnemonic: Lo plus an adjective is a noun with no noun in it.

sentences.display: Me alegro mucho de que vengas hoy a mi casa.
sentences.cue: I am really glad you are coming to my house today.
sentences.literal: Me I-gladden much of that you-may-come today to my house.

words.note: Takes de before its que: me alegro DE que. The de is not optional and dropping it is the second commonest error in this pattern.

sentences.trap: English says I am glad you are coming, with a plain indicative. Spanish cannot: the moment there is a second subject, the verb after que goes subjunctive.
sentences.sound: Alegro is a-LE-gro, and the g is hard, as in the English word grow.

variations.cue: I am glad you are coming.
variations.changed: The pattern reduced to its bones — trigger, de que, subjunctive — with nothing else in the way.

mistake.display: Me alegro de que vienes hoy.
mistake.why: Vienes is the indicative. Me alegro de que is a trigger of emotion with two subjects in it, so the verb after que must be vengas — this is the single commonest error of the level.

sentences.usage: Neutral, and warm without being effusive. It is what you say to somebody who has just told you good news about themselves.

sentences.display: Me alegro de que haya venido usted a la boda.
sentences.cue: I am glad that you came to the wedding.
sentences.literal: Me I-gladden of that there-may-have come you to the wedding.

words.note: L4-M3 taught venido and the perfect. Haya is the subjunctive of that same helper, and haya venido is the already-done version of vengas.

sentences.trap: The trigger is present and the thing wished about is finished, so the subjunctive goes perfect rather than past. Nothing in the trigger moves.
sentences.sound: Haya has a silent h and the y is a soft consonant: A-ya, two syllables.

variations.display: Me alegro de que haya venido.
variations.changed: Without usted, which is how it is usually said — the form itself already says who.

mistake.display: Me alegro de que vino usted a la boda.
mistake.why: Vino is the indicative past. When the trigger is an emotion the mood cannot be indicative at all, and because the coming is finished the form wanted is haya venido.

sentences.usage: Formal, with usted — this is the sentence for a wedding, a leaving lunch or a panel, said to somebody you would not call tu.
sentences.mnemonic: Still happening takes vengas; already happened takes haya venido.

sentences.display: Me molestó mucho que dijeran eso de mi hermana ayer.
sentences.cue: It really bothered me that they said that about my sister yesterday.
sentences.literal: Me it-bothered much that they-might-say that of my sister yesterday.

words.note: L3-M6 taught me molesta in the present. This is the same row in the past, and it is the tense of the TRIGGER that decides everything after que.
Imperfect subjunctive of decir, built on the irregular stem dij-. The -se twin dijesen means exactly the same, as L5-M3 showed.
The same form from hacer, on the stem hic-. Both are built from the they-form of the simple past, which is where every imperfect subjunctive comes from.

sentences.trap: A past trigger drags the whole clause back with it. You do not get to choose the tense after que; me molesta takes digan and me molesto takes dijeran.
sentences.sound: Dijeran is di-HE-ran: the j is the throaty h of Spanish, and the stress is on the middle syllable.

variations.cue: It bothered me that he did that.
variations.changed: The same past trigger with a different verb under it, so the shape shows through rather than the words.

mistake.why: Dijeron is the plain past indicative. Under a trigger of feeling the clause is subjunctive whatever the tense, so a past trigger takes dijeran.

sentences.usage: Neutral. Said about something reported rather than to the person who did it; saying it to their face is a different conversation and a different register.
sentences.mnemonic: The trigger picks the tense, and you only pick the trigger.

sentences.display: En el fondo, la gente quiere libertad, justicia y respeto, nada más.
sentences.cue: Deep down, people want freedom, justice and respect, nothing more.
sentences.literal: In the bottom, the people it-wants freedom, justice and respect, nothing more.

words.cue: deep down · when it comes down to it
words.note: The frame Spanish hedges with instead of hedging the claim. It goes at the front, with a comma, and what follows it is stated flat.
Feminine, like every Spanish noun ending in -dad: la libertad. Readable on sight, which is why the module can afford three of these in one line.
Covers both the courts and plain fairness, so no es justo means that is not fair long before it means anything legal.
El respeto, masculine. Not to be read as the verb respeto, I respect — same letters, and the article is what tells you which one is meant.

sentences.trap: En el fondo hedges the frame, not the claim. Everything after the comma is said flat, with no softening at all, and softening it as well is what makes a learner sound evasive.
sentences.sound: Libertad ends on a soft d that in Spain is barely there — li-ber-TA. The stress is on the last syllable in all three nouns here.

variations.display: En el fondo, todo es más difícil.
variations.cue: Deep down, it is all harder than that.
variations.changed: The frame carrying an ordinary sentence, to show that it is not tied to abstract nouns.

mistake.display: Creo que en el fondo la gente quiere quizás libertad.
mistake.why: Hedging twice. Spanish puts the softening in the frame and then commits; stacking creo que, en el fondo and quizas is the English habit and it reads as having no view at all.

sentences.usage: Neutral, and this is the two-in-the-morning register: the frame buys you the right to state something large without seeming to lecture.
sentences.mnemonic: Hedge the frame, then say the thing straight.

sentences.display: Lo difícil no es hablar; lo difícil es escuchar de verdad.
sentences.cue: The hard part is not talking; the hard part is really listening.
sentences.literal: The difficult not it-is to-speak; the difficult it-is to-listen of truth.

words.cue: the hard part · what is difficult
words.note: L3-M3 taught dificil. The same lo trick as lo importante, and the adjective stays masculine singular however many people it is about.
Listening on purpose, as against oir, which is hearing whether you meant to. Takes a direct object with no preposition: escuchar a alguien.

sentences.trap: Lo never agrees with anything. It is not el and not la, and it stays lo even when the hard part is a woman, a group or a plural.
sentences.sound: Dificil is di-FI-cil, stressed in the middle, and the written accent is what says so; without it the word would be read di-fi-CIL.

variations.changed: One half of the contrast, which is complete on its own — the pattern does not need a second clause.

mistake.display: La difícil es escuchar de verdad.
mistake.why: There is no gender here to agree with. Lo is the neuter article and takes a masculine singular adjective always, whatever the sentence is about.

sentences.usage: Neutral. The two-part contrast — lo X no es A, lo X es B — is how a claim is sharpened in Spanish without raising the voice.
sentences.mnemonic: Lo is neuter and agrees with nobody.

sentences.display: Es una pena que no vinieran a la boda de mi hermana.
sentences.cue: It is a shame they did not come to my sister's wedding.
sentences.literal: It-is a pity that not they-might-come to the wedding of my sister.

words.cue: it is a shame · what a pity
words.note: A trigger of value with no person in it, so it behaves exactly like the ones that have. Que pena is the same feeling as an exclamation.
Imperfect subjunctive of venir, on the stem vin-. The trigger is present here and the clause is past, because the not-coming is over.

sentences.trap: A present trigger does not force a present subjunctive. It forces the subjunctive; the tense inside it still tracks when the thing happened.
sentences.sound: Vinieran is vi-NYE-ran; the ie is one glide and the stress sits on it.

variations.display: Es una pena que no vinieran.
variations.cue: It is a shame they did not come.
variations.changed: The trigger and its clause with nothing after them, which is the whole pattern.

mistake.display: Es una pena que no vinieron.
mistake.why: Vinieron is the plain past. Es una pena is a value judgement and every clause under one is subjunctive, so the form is vinieran.

sentences.usage: Neutral, and softer than it looks: es una pena is regret rather than blame, and it is what you say about people you are still fond of.
sentences.mnemonic: The trigger sets the mood; the facts still set the tense.

sentences.display: Me alegro de escuchar, y me alegro de que tú escuches también.
sentences.cue: I am glad to be listening, and I am glad that you are listening too.
sentences.literal: Me I-gladden of to-listen, and me I-gladden of that you you-may-listen too.

words.note: The tu cell of the same subjunctive S01 used for la gente. It is here only because the second half changes subject; the first half needs no such form at all.

sentences.trap: This is the module's minimal pair inside one sentence. Same subject on both sides takes de plus the plain infinitive; a new subject takes de que plus the subjunctive. Nothing else moves.
sentences.sound: Escuches is es-CU-ches, and the final -s is fully pronounced; it is what separates you listen from he listens.

variations.cue: I am glad to be coming.
variations.changed: The same-subject half with a different verb: no que anywhere, and the infinitive straight after de.

mistake.display: Me alegro de que escucho también.
mistake.why: One subject on both sides, so there is no que at all: me alegro de escuchar. Spanish never puts que between a feeling and the person already having it.

sentences.usage: Informal, tu — the two-in-the-morning conversation the whole module is built for. It is a compliment, and a warm one.
sentences.mnemonic: One subject takes the infinitive; two subjects take que.

sentences.display: Lo bueno es que hoy el mundo puede hablar de estos valores.
sentences.cue: The good thing is that today the world can talk about these values.
sentences.literal: The good it-is that today the world it-can to-speak of these values.

words.note: L1-M10 taught bueno. Lo bueno and lo malo are the pair a Spanish speaker weighs a thing with: lo bueno de esto es que.
Todo el mundo means everybody, not the whole planet, so the article is doing more work here than it looks like.
Plural in this sense, always: los valores. In the singular el valor is worth, or courage, which is a different word to a Spanish ear.

sentences.trap: Es que here is indicative, not subjunctive. Lo bueno es que states a fact about the world; lo importante es que in S01 states a requirement, and only the second takes the subjunctive.
sentences.sound: Valores is ba-LO-res: the v is the same sound as b, and the stress is on the middle syllable.

variations.display: Lo bueno es que el mundo puede cambiar.
variations.cue: The good thing is that the world can change.
variations.changed: The same frame carrying a plainer claim, so the pattern shows without the vocabulary.

mistake.display: Lo bueno es que hoy el mundo pueda hablar.
mistake.why: Pueda would make it a wish or a requirement. Lo bueno es que reports something true, and reporting is indicative — this is the boundary between S01 and this sentence.

sentences.usage: Neutral, and usable in front of an audience: this is the panel half of the module, where lo bueno es que opens a considered answer.
sentences.mnemonic: Lo importante demands, so it takes the subjunctive; lo bueno reports, so it does not.

sentences.display: ¿Tú crees que la vida tiene sentido? En el fondo, creo que sí.
sentences.cue: Do you think life has meaning? Deep down, I think it does.
sentences.literal: You you-believe that the life it-has sense? In the bottom, I-believe that yes.

words.note: Feminine: la vida. Asi es la vida is the fixed phrase every learner meets first, and it is the same word.
Tener sentido is to make sense, of an argument as much as of a life. It is also the sentido of L5-M4's sentido pesame, felt rather than meant.

sentences.trap: Crees que takes the indicative because a question about belief is still a question about a fact. It is the NEGATIVE, no creo que, that flips to the subjunctive — and that belongs to L4-M5, not here.
sentences.sound: Sentido is sen-TI-do, and the final d is soft, closer to the th of the English word this.

variations.cue: Do you think it makes sense?
variations.changed: The everyday use of the same phrase, about an argument or a plan rather than about a life.

mistake.display: ¿Tú crees que la vida tenga sentido?
mistake.why: A plain question about what somebody believes is indicative: crees que tiene. The subjunctive would arrive with a negative in front, no creo que tenga, which is a different sentence.

sentences.usage: Informal, tu, and this is the hour the module was written for. It is not small talk; asked of somebody you met an hour ago it lands as strange rather than deep.
sentences.mnemonic: Believing takes the indicative; it is doubting that changes the mood.
